nodes.label: Jonathan Israel
nodes.description: A historian of the Dutch Republic, European Jews and the Enlightenment. In his 2023 interview with Florian Louis, Israel argues that Spinoza’s early reception and clandestine networks were central to a radical current combining criticism of religious authority with political equality. He treats its relation to moderate Enlightenment as a fundamental explanatory division. This remains his contested interpretation: the interview names opponents, including Antoine Lilti, and records his rejection of their objections. The entry does not turn his thesis into a consensus or assign every Enlightenment thinker to one camp.

nodes.scope_note: Selected 2023 primary interview answers on reception and radical/moderate distinction read; IAS bibliography checked. Complete selected books and critics’ original arguments unread. A history-of-ideas contribution does not establish membership in the Cambridge contextualist school.

nodes.label: Geoffrey Parker
nodes.description: A historian of early modern Europe, warfare and the Spanish monarchy. His work on the Army of Flanders investigates the logistics of power, while his military-revolution interpretation expands the problem beyond battlefield tactics to fortification, scale and chronology. Rogers’s participant-editor account presents this as a continuing debate rather than a settled technological explanation. Parker’s own Ohio State research statement explains his later attempt to connect seventeenth-century political upheaval with climatic change across regions. That is his global explanatory project, not independent verification of every demographic estimate or causal claim.

nodes.label: T. M. Devine
nodes.description: A historian of Scottish social and economic change whose work connects Highland transformation and national synthesis with Atlantic commerce. His 2011 essay asks how slavery-based economies contributed to Scotland’s development rather than assuming that the scale of direct slave-trading voyages answers that question. National framing itself remains disputed: Graeme Morton and Trevor Griffiths ask whether the title and container of The Scottish Nation reproduce a restrictive national perspective. Their criticism accompanies this entry; it does not negate Devine’s comparative interests or turn national history into nationalist allegiance.

nodes.label: Richard J. Evans
nodes.description: A historian of modern Germany who also examines the methods and public responsibilities of historical inquiry. In Defence of History defends research and evidence while allowing that outside criticism can expose historians’ unexamined assumptions; its checked introduction does not stand for every later argument. Death in Hamburg connects disease with social inequality and civic government, as the Wolfson account explains. His work on the Third Reich and service as an expert witness in the Irving trial are distinct parts of his scholarship. Institutional professional records establish that scope without substituting a film or a court role for a reading of the books.

nodes.label: Thomas W. Laqueur
nodes.description: A cultural historian of bodies, sexuality and death. His Berkeley interview connects seemingly natural bodily states with the historical meanings people give them. The Work of the Dead asks what the care and naming of the dead do for the living, including making social relationships persist through time. Making Sex and Solitary Sex address other histories of embodied life. These accounts retain the distinction between an author’s stated interpretive questions and verification of the books’ complete arguments; no universal model of sex or mourning is inferred.

nodes.label: Charles S. Maier
nodes.description: A historian of modern Europe whose work connects political economy, territorial power and the public uses of the past. In his research statement, Maier asks how control of bordered space changes and how empires make or disrupt international order. A separate cluster of questions concerns collective memory, reparations and political trials after repression. His account places these inquiries alongside comparative and contemporary history rather than treating one national case as a universal template. These are his stated research questions; the selected books are bibliographically checked but unread in full.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Unmasterable Past (1988); “Consigning the Twentieth Century to History” (2000); Among Empires (2006); Once Within Borders (2016).
nodes.scope_note: Primary Harvard research statement read, plus selected 2017 interview opening and institutional bibliography. Books and the complete 2000 article unread. Territoriality is a problem to investigate, not a claim that globalization simply eliminates states.

nodes.label: E. H. Carr
nodes.description: A historian of Soviet Russia, diplomat and international-relations writer whose What Is History? made historical selection and interpretation explicit problems. Its first chapter treats research and interpretation as reciprocal and refuses to make all accounts equally valid. That position is distinct from simply denying facts or claiming that the past is whatever a historian chooses. The Twenty Years’ Crisis and the multivolume Soviet history belong to different inquiries. This entry does not infer their complete political or theoretical arguments from the methodological lectures.

nodes.label: Judith R. Walkowitz
nodes.description: A historian of modern Britain whose work joins women’s history with studies of sexuality, urban culture and political conflict. In her own Johns Hopkins account, Prostitution and Victorian Society examines medical and police regulation, while City of Dreadful Delight studies how narratives of sexual danger circulated through late-Victorian London. Nights Out shifts the inquiry to the social encounters and inequalities of cosmopolitan Soho. These are connected questions about power and representation, rather than a claim that London formed a harmonious melting pot or that cultural narratives alone explain every social change.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Prostitution and Victorian Society (1980); City of Dreadful Delight (1992); Nights Out: Life in Cosmopolitan London (2012).
nodes.scope_note: First-person institutional biography and Nights Out research account read; complete books unread. Method claims remain the author’s retrospective framing, not independent verification of all archival arguments.

nodes.label: Paul Kennedy
nodes.description: A historian of international power, strategy and political economy. His work connects military capabilities with the economic resources and political choices that sustain them. In a 2009 Yale discussion, Kennedy treats international institutions as dependent on states’ leadership and warns that an economic crisis can crowd other global problems off their agendas. The contribution here is that historically informed inquiry into power and institutional capacity. The entry does not turn his earlier great-power study into a mechanical prediction of national decline or adopt the panel’s contemporary forecasts as facts.

nodes.label: T. C. Smout
nodes.description: A historian of Scottish society who later helped establish environmental history as an institutional and interpretive field. His green-consciousness lecture examines changes in appreciation of Highland landscapes while refusing to make appreciation of nature simply a new import from outside Scotland. His social syntheses also form part of a debate about the nation as the frame of historical writing, discussed by Morton and Griffiths. Those bounded readings connect social and environmental questions without making the landscape timeless or treating a national synthesis as political allegiance.
